source_text: CAPUT DECIMUM QUARTUM, De vita Dei. Conveniunt et absolutam perfectionem Dei, ut entis, negative declarant: nunc sequuntur attributa secundi generis, quae affirmative notant summam perfectionem Dei, ut spiritualiter viventis, hoc est, evidenter respectu vitae intelligentis. Atque haec veluti principia actionum existunt in Deo; qua de causa etiam creaturis tribuuntur, non quidem ut in Deo sunt, cum gradu supereminentiae, sed suo et limitato modo, per participationem videlicet et secundum aliquam similitudinem, quae tamen a Dei perfectione infinite deficit. Hinc est quod homines ad imaginem Dei conditi, Gen. I.27, et naturae divinae consortes fieri, II Pet. I.4, dicuntur. Sunt autem haec secundi generis attributa affirmativa, quia primo et formaliter perfectionem positivam indicant, ac propterea etiam per affirmationem seu positionem potius a nobis concipiuntur et exponuntur. Modus tamen supereminentiae, qui illis adjicitur, semper negationem includit. Vita Dei est summa illius perfectio, qua essentia ipsius excellenter actuosa est.
english: CHAPTER FOURTEEN. On the life of God.

The former attributes agree and declare God's absolute perfection as a being negatively: now there follow attributes of the second genus, which affirmatively note God's highest perfection as spiritually living — that is, evidently with respect to intelligent life. And these exist in God as principles of actions; for which cause they are also attributed to creatures, not indeed as they are in God with the degree of supereminence, but in their own limited mode, namely by participation and according to some likeness, which yet infinitely falls short of God's perfection.

Hence it is that men are said to be made in God's image (Genesis 1:27) and to become partakers of the divine nature (2 Peter 1:4). But these second-genus attributes are affirmative, because first and formally they indicate a positive perfection, and therefore are also rather conceived and expounded by us through affirmation or position. Yet the mode of supereminence added to them always includes a negation. The life of God is His highest perfection, by which His essence is excellently active.

source_text: Vita Dei ambigue dicitur, vel qua ipse vivit in se, vel qua vivit in nobis. De hac Paulus loquitur Ephes. IV.18, dicens gentes alienatas esse a vita Dei. De qua etiam Irenaeus lib. V. adversus haereses cap. XIII: Vita, inquit, hominis duplex est, naturalis et spiritualis. Naturalis est vita illa quam habemus per primam generationem in Adamo, nihilque aliud est quam functio animae rationalis in movendo, sentiendo, ratiocinando; de hac dicitur Act. XVII.28: Per ipsum vivimus, movemur et sumus. Vita spiritualis est illa quam habemus per secundam generationem in Christo, nihilque aliud est quam motus perfectus ab actione Spiritus sancti, qui hominis regenerati tanquam anima est: atque haec est illa vita quae ad Ephesios dicitur vita Dei, et II Cor. IV.11 vita Jesu. Non de hac, sed de illa hic potissimum agimus, qua videlicet Deus vivit in se, quae Deus ipse est, et a nobis concipitur tanquam secundum naturae divinae momentum. Materiale quidem etiam in hoc attributo idem est quod in aliis, summa nempe Dei perfectio; formale vero est in positione modi spiritualis vitae supereminentissimi, quo Deus in se et extra se actuosus est.
english: The life of God is said ambiguously: either that by which He Himself lives in Himself, or that by which He lives in us. Of the latter Paul speaks in Ephesians 4:18, saying the Gentiles are alienated from the life of God. Of which also Irenaeus, Against Heresies book V chapter 13: The life of man, he says, is twofold, natural and spiritual.

Natural is that life which we have through the first generation in Adam, and is nothing other than the function of the rational soul in moving, sensing, and reasoning; of this it is said in Acts 17:28, In Him we live and move and are. Spiritual is that life which we have through the second generation in Christ, and is nothing other than perfect motion from the action of the Holy Spirit, who is as it were the soul of the regenerate man: and this is that life which to the Ephesians is called the life of God, and in 2 Corinthians 4:11 the life of Jesus.

Not of this, but of that we chiefly treat here — namely that by which God lives in Himself, which is God Himself, and is conceived by us as the second moment of the divine nature. The material in this attribute also is the same as in the others, namely God's highest perfection; but the formal consists in the position of the most supereminent mode of spiritual life by which God is active in Himself and outside Himself.

source_text: Sed Deum vivere ita probamus. PRIMO, a luculentis sacrae Scripturae testimoniis. Haec enim vitam illi disertim tribuit: Gen. XVI.14; Num. XIV.21; Deut. XXXII.40; I Sam. XVII.26; Psal. XXXVI.10; Psal. XLII.3; Jer. IV.2; Ezech. XXXIII.11; Matth. XVI.16; Act. XIV.15; Rom. IX.26; Hebr. III.12; Hebr. X.31. SECUNDO, infinita Dei perfectione. Qui infinita perfectione est, is vivit. Deus est infinita perfectione. Ergo Deus vivit. TERTIO, actionibus Dei internis. Qui intelligit, vult et potest, is vivit. Deus intelligit, vult, potest. Ergo Deus vivit. QUARTO, actionibus Dei internis quae vulgo ad intra dicuntur. Qui est gignens et genitus, spirans et procedens, is vivit. Atqui Deus est gignens et genitus, spirans et procedens. Ergo Deus vivit — Joh. V.26. QUINTO, actionibus Dei externis. Qui omnia vivificat, is vivit. Atqui Deus omnia vivificat — Gen. II.7; Num. XVI.22; I Sam. II.6; Psal. XXXVI.10; Act. XVII.25; I Tim. VI.13. Ergo Deus vivit.
english: But that God lives we prove thus. FIRST, from the clear testimonies of sacred Scripture. For this distinctly attributes life to Him: Genesis 16:14; Numbers 14:21; Deuteronomy 32:40; 1 Samuel 17:26; Psalm 36:10; Psalm 42:3; Jeremiah 4:2; Ezekiel 33:11; Matthew 16:16; Acts 14:15; Romans 9:26; Hebrews 3:12; Hebrews 10:31.

SECOND, from God's infinite perfection. Whoever is of infinite perfection lives. God is of infinite perfection. Therefore God lives. THIRD, from God's inward actions. Whoever understands, wills, and can, lives. God understands, wills, can. Therefore God lives.

FOURTH, from God's inward actions commonly called ad intra. Whoever is begetting and begotten, breathing and proceeding, lives. But God is begetting and begotten, breathing and proceeding. Therefore God lives — John 5:26. FIFTH, from God's outward actions. Whoever vivifies all things lives. But God vivifies all things — Genesis 2:7; Numbers 16:22; 1 Samuel 2:6; Psalm 36:10; Acts 17:25; 1 Timothy 6:13. Therefore God lives.

source_text: SEXTO, his accedit consensus orthodoxae antiquitatis. Dionysio qui ab Areopago denominatur Deus est autzoe, ipsavita et autzoos per se vivens, aeizoon aeternum vivens; et juxta cum hoc Gregorio, archezoon vitae auctor. Irenaeus: Deus vita est et incorruptela et veritas. Cyrillus Alexandrinus: Inest, inquit, oportet vero Deo incorruptio et interitus vacuitas, imo et ut vivat, et vitam tribuere possit his quibus vitam velit inesse. Basilius Magnus; Augustinus: Nulla vita est quae non sit ex Deo, quia Deus utique summa vita est et ipse fons vitae. SEPTIMO, subscribunt philosophi gentiles. Aristoteles Metaph. XII: Dicimus itaque Deum sempiternum optimumque vivens esse. Quare vita et aevum continuum et aeternum Deo inest. Orpheus; Hermes; Zeno Cittieus Deum animal dixit, id est vivens immortale. DISCEDIT hic etiam Conradus Vorstius Notis ad disp. III p.247, inquiens videri aliquid in Deo diversitatis inesse, ut aliud sit ipsa Dei substantia vivens, aliud vita seu vis illa per quam vivit. Sed modeste sapiunt qui res divinas bene sapiunt, nec Deo tribuunt ea quorum similitudo in creaturis exstat, nisi cum modo supereminentiae ac negatione omnimodae imperfectionis.
english: SIXTH, to these is added the consent of orthodox antiquity. To Dionysius named from the Areopagus God is self-life and living through Himself, eternally living; and with him Gregory, the archetypal author of life. Irenaeus: God is life and incorruption and truth. Cyril of Alexandria: There must be in the true God incorruption and freedom from destruction, and indeed that He live and can grant life to those in whom He wills life to be. Basil the Great; Augustine: There is no life that is not from God, because God is indeed the highest life and Himself the fountain of life.

SEVENTH, the Gentile philosophers subscribe. Aristotle, Metaphysics XII: We say therefore that God is a living being everlasting and best. Therefore life and continuous eternal age are in God. Orpheus; Hermes; Zeno of Citium called God an animal, that is an immortal living being.

Here also Conrad Vorstius departs in Notes on Disputation III p. 247, saying it seems some diversity is in God, so that one thing is God's living substance itself, another the life or force by which He lives. But they wisely know who know divine things well, and attribute to God those things whose likeness exists in creatures only with the mode of supereminence and negation of every imperfection.

source_text: II. Sunt autem de his secundi generis attributis, adeoque vita Dei, tenendae REGULAE. 1. Attributa secundi generis in Deo cum pictantur, ad normam et formam attributorum primi generis sunt exigenda, ut ei tribuantur infinite, perfectissime, simplicissime, immutabiliter. Sic Deus vivus dicitur infinite perfectissimeque, quia nihil vitae illius deest et omni termino ac limite caret extensive et intensive; simplicissime, quia vita illius est prorsus incomposita et ipsissima Dei essentia actuosa; immutabiliter, quia ut Deus non coepit unquam vivere, ita nec definet. 2. Quicquid his attributis simile et analogum in rebus creatis deprehenditur, id finitum, imperfectum, mixtum ac motus mutationisque vicibus obnoxium, accidentarium denique et adventitium est. 3. Ex hujus generis attributis Deum primam omnium veram causam esse vel maxime intelligitur — unde primum vivens appellari potest. 4. Vita sua Deus verus distinguitur ab idolis — Jos. III.10; Jer. II.13; X.9-10; Dan. VI.26; I Thess. I.9. 5. Propter vitam suam Deus colendus est — timor, Deut. VI.13; honor et adoratio, Hebr. IX.14; Apoc. IV.9; jusjurandum, Jer. IV.2; spes, I Tim. VI.17. III. Vita Dei consistit in intellectu omnia penetrante, voluntate prorsus libera, agendique potentia prompta cui non est resistere. Hae sunt quasi facultates Dei vitales, ad quas omnia attributa referimus.
english: II. But concerning these second-genus attributes, and so concerning the life of God, RULES are to be held. 1. When second-genus attributes are painted in God, they are to be measured to the norm and form of first-genus attributes, so that they are attributed to Him infinitely, most perfectly, most simply, immutably. So God is called living infinitely and most perfectly, because nothing of His life is wanting and He lacks every bound extensively and intensively; most simply, because His life is wholly uncomposed and God's very active essence; immutably, because as God never began to live, so neither will He cease.

2. Whatever like and analogous to these attributes is found in created things is finite, imperfect, mixed, subject to turns of motion and change, and finally accidental and adventitious. 3. From attributes of this genus it is understood especially that God is the first true cause of all — whence He can be called the first living. 4. By His life the true God is distinguished from idols — Joshua 3:10; Jeremiah 2:13; 10:9-10; Daniel 6:26; 1 Thessalonians 1:9. 5. Because of His life God is to be worshiped — fear, Deuteronomy 6:13; honor and adoration, Hebrews 9:14; Revelation 4:9; oath, Jeremiah 4:2; hope, 1 Timothy 6:17.

III. The life of God consists in an intellect penetrating all things, a will wholly free, and a ready power of acting which none can resist. These are as it were God's vital faculties, to which we refer all attributes.
